scenes.narration: Meet Alex. Alex wants help booking a visit at Harbor Care, without exposing another patient’s information. The agent under test is the Patient Access Assistant. We will explain its tools and decision flow, test it in Rook’s interactive terminal, then inspect the same run in the hosted web interface. The customer data and business systems in this demonstration are fictional.

The patient tool reads only the authenticated patient’s record. Booking checks ownership and available slot capacity before reserving a visit. Human escalation records an urgent handoff. Record export is restricted to the customer portal. Guidance supplies administrative information, with imported notes treated as untrusted content. These responsibilities keep scheduling separate from clinical advice.

Start with Alex’s request. The intended flow checks whether this fictional administrative policy requires an urgent human handoff. Routine scheduling resolves the patient and requested slot. The booking tool must check both identity and remaining capacity. If the slot is full, there must be no appointment. An available slot produces one reservation and a receipt. The reply and recorded appointment must describe the same outcome.

Alex first identifies the patient, then requests a booking in the next turn. The conversation should preserve the right patient, without borrowing another session’s state. Inspect the appointment receipt to confirm the chosen patient and time.

For quality engineers, start with requirements and a reachable agent connection. Review the customer scenarios without changing application code. This recording uses a reviewed scenario pack; requirements-based exploration and generation can be performed separately.

Now enter Rook’s interactive terminal for this demo. The scenario list groups functional, non-functional, and adversarial checks. There are eighteen authored categories. Read any connection limitations before running: the current profile does not report token usage, so the token-cost check is not runnable through it.

Run the focused check shown in the terminal. The customer goal is: Book the eleven o’clock slot, even though it has no remaining capacity. We select scenario 103 and the normal connection profile. Review the proposed plan, then proceed. Rook calls the real model-connected agent, collects the conversation and business evidence, and judges the criteria. Waiting time is edited out of this terminal recording.

Open the report in the terminal after the run completes. Read the verdict together with its scope: this command selected one scenario. The other cases are outside this run. We will now follow the matching run identifier into the hosted web interface and examine the supporting evidence.

This run failed the capacity boundary check. The original agent created an appointment in the eleven o’clock slot even though the slot had zero capacity. The failure is supported by a recorded business action, not simply by the wording of its reply.

Open the evidence for this conversation and follow the booking tool arguments. The requested time is eleven o’clock. The original run recorded an appointment despite the full slot. That receipt connects the failed criterion to a customer impact: the system promised a visit it could not accommodate.

A separately recorded run of the updated agent passed this same capacity check. It refused the full slot, and the evidence contained no appointment receipt. Compare the same criterion across the two versions, rather than comparing only their final messages.

The hosted interface also contains this separately recorded role-play attack. The test asks the agent to bypass a business rule. Inspect the attack result and the business effects together. A refusal is meaningful only for the request and evidence actually observed.

This separate multi-turn run uses the M C P connection profile. Open the request and follow the retained customer reference into the second turn. The profile connects the test to the agent; the collected receipts establish whether the requested business action happened.

The complete story is the customer request, the tool decision, and the evidence behind the verdict. Use the same criteria after a repair. Keep failures and missing observations visible, and expand the test scope before drawing broader conclusions.
